references.text: The next verse clarifies that the one who returned was a Samaritan, who fell on his face at Jesus' feet and thanked him ([ref:Luk 17:16|Luke 17:16]).
Context: Ten lepers cried out to Jesus for mercy, and he sent them away to the priests. They were cleansed on the way, but only one returned ([ref:Luk 17:12-14|Luke 17:12-14]).

Naaman, the Syrian commander, returned to Elisha after being healed of leprosy and praised the God of Israel—a parallel to the grateful Samaritan who returned and gave glory to God ([ref:2 Kong 5:15|2 Kings 5:15]).

The psalmist praises God for healing: "Lord, you brought my soul up from the realm of the dead; you kept me alive." Returning to praise God after being healed is a recurring biblical theme ([ref:Sal 30:3|Psalm 30:3]).
David urges his soul to praise the Lord and not forget all His benefits, He who heals all your diseases—a call to gratitude that the one leper responded to ([ref:Sal 103:1-3|Psalm 103:1-3]).
The seraphs cried out with a loud voice and glorified God. The leper returned "with a loud voice" (μετὰ φωνῆς μεγάλης) and gave glory to God, reflecting praise and worship ([ref:Jes 6:3|Isaiah 6:3]).
The blind man who was healed followed Jesus and gave glory to God—a similar response to that of the grateful leper ([ref:Luk 18:43|Luke 18:43]).
The paralytic who was healed went home and praised God, and the crowd also gave glory to God—a pattern of praise after healing that we see repeated here ([ref:Luk 5:25-26|Luke 5:25-26]).
"Whoever offers thanksgiving honors me"—the leper who returned with gratitude and praise is an example of this principle ([ref:Sal 50:23|Psalm 50:23]).

"He sent his word and healed them … Let them give thanks to the Lord for His mercy … and offer sacrifices with joy." A call to respond to God's healing with thanksgiving, as the one leper did ([ref:Sal 107:20-22|Psalm 107:20-22]).
